setup.zh: 马家花三百两给马小宝买了一张荐书。那天夜里，爹从墙上摘下了那张弓；娘给了你针线和一个空钱袋。
setup.en: The Mas spend three hundred taels on a letter of recommendation for Ma Xiaobao. That night Father takes the bow down from the wall; Mother gives you needle and thread and an empty purse.

recap.zh: 爹把爷爷的弓给了你，娘给了你针线和一个空钱袋：「你自己挣满它。」
recap.en: Father gave you grandfather's bow, and Mother needle and thread and an empty purse: "Fill it yourself."

zh: 娘的针线，和一个空钱袋。
en: Father takes the old bow down from the wall.
Mother's needle and thread, and an empty purse.

story.zh:
九月初九之前，整个县城都知道了沉鼎观开山门的消息，马家自然也知道了。

马家老爷托了县里那个做书吏的远房表侄，花了整整三百两银子，给马小宝弄到了一张「荐书」。三百两银子，是沈家一百多年的租。

马三在村口的酒桌上喝得满脸通红，拍着桌子嚷嚷：「有荐书，灵根差一点也收！我家小宝，将来是要做仙师的！到时候，我就是仙师他爹！」

村里人齐声道：「恭喜三爷！」

马三一拍桌子，又道：「到时候，蒙山上的风——」

村里人齐声接口，十分熟练：「姓马！」

小满蹲在自家门口，剥着一颗栗子，一句话没说。他瞧着那一桌人，瞧着马小宝的腮帮子一鼓一鼓的，忽然想起打谷场上那首歌来。他没唱出声，只在心里把末一句过了一遍。

胸口的木牌热了一下。他小声道：「我知道。三百两。记账。」

那天夜里，小满把自己的决定告诉了爹娘。

他爹沉默了很久。他坐在炕沿上，一只手按着膝盖，一只手搁在炕桌上，指头一下一下地敲着桌面，敲得极慢，像是在数着什么。小满知道他在数什么。他在数墙角那十七个盆，在数这些年交给马家的租，在数那两亩一年比一年薄的地；他还在数，从石坳村到泗水，有多少里路，路上有多少他照看不到的地方。

然后他站了起来，一瘸一拐地走到墙边，把那张缠着牛筋的旧弓摘了下来，捧在手里，看了一会儿，放在儿子面前，说道：「你爷爷的。你拿着。」

小满一愣：「……爹，这话听着像骂人。」

「不许瞎说。」他爹把弓往他怀里一塞，「你爷爷的弓。」

小满抱着那张弓。弓背上十七道牛筋，秋天松了的那一道，他按回去以后，他爹又拿新牛筋重缠过了，缠得紧紧的。他抬起头来道：「爹，那家里——」

「家里有我。」他爹道，「膝盖不行，手还行，种两亩地饿不死。」

他爹又道：「这弓，你拉过一回了。拉得不错。」他顿了一顿，「往后，一个人拉。一个人拉，就没人在你身后说先看风了。你得自己说。」

小满道：「先看风，后看鹿。」

他爹道：「嗯。」他想了一想，又道：「还有一句，我没跟你说过。」

小满竖起耳朵。

他爹道：「看不清风，就别拉。」他拿手按了按弓背，「一张弓，一辈子射得出去几支箭？射出去的，收不回来。不拉，不丢人。」

他爹顿了一顿，又道：「到了仙家门派，要守人家的规矩。要老实。别跟人争——」

小满他娘道：「他爹。」

他爹便不说了。

他娘从怀里摸出一个小布包，塞进小满手里。小满打开一看，是一套针线：一个顶针，三根针，一卷黑线，一卷白线，针插在一块碎布上，整整齐齐。还有一个钱袋，青布缝的，针脚细细密密，袋口穿着一根红绳。

钱袋是空的。

他娘道：「针线。衣裳破了，自己补。」她拿指头点了点那个钱袋，「钱袋是空的。你自己，挣满它。」

他娘看着他，又道：「你爹的话，你听一半。」

他爹在炕沿上咳了一声。他娘没理他。

「要守规矩——对。要老实——对好人老实。别跟人争——」说到这里，她停住了。她伸出手来，把他的衣领翻好。那衣领是她前几天拆了又缝的，翻过来，里子朝外，看着便新了些。她把衣领翻好了，又抻了抻，抻平了，才道：

「争得过，再争。」

屋里静了。油灯的火苗跳了一跳。

小满看着他娘。他娘也看着他，脸上什么表情也没有，就像在说今儿的粥稀了点。可她那只翻衣领的手，翻完了，没有马上收回去，在他的肩膀上，停了一停。

小满后来走过许多地方，见过许多人，听过许多大人物说的大道理。可这辈子教他怎么活的话，统共只有这五个字。
story.en:
Before the ninth of the ninth month the whole county town knew Chending Temple was opening its gate, and naturally the Mas knew too.

Master Ma went through that distant nephew, the county clerk, and spent a full three hundred taels to get Ma Xiaobao a "letter of recommendation". Three hundred taels was over a hundred years of the Shens' rent.

Ma San drank himself scarlet at the wine table at the village gate, banging the table and bawling: "With a letter of recommendation, a bit of a bad root still gets you in! My Xiaobao's going to be an immortal master! And then I'll be an immortal master's dad!"

The villagers said in chorus: "Congratulations, Third Master!"

Ma San banged the table again. "And then — the wind on Mount Meng —"

The villagers took it up in chorus, well practised: "— is named Ma!"

Xiaoman squatted at his own door peeling a chestnut and said not a word. He watched that table of people, watched Ma Xiaobao's cheeks bulging, and suddenly thought of the song on the threshing floor. He didn't sing it aloud; he just ran the last line through his head.

The token at his chest warmed. He said softly: "I know. Three hundred taels. It goes in the books."

That night Xiaoman told his parents his decision.

His father was silent a long time. He sat on the edge of the kang, one hand on his knee, the other on the kang table, tapping the tabletop with a finger, very slowly, as if counting something. Xiaoman knew what he was counting. The seventeen basins in the corner, the rent paid to the Mas all these years, the two mu of land thinner every year; and how many li from Shi'ao Village to the Si River, and how many places along the road he couldn't watch over.

Then he stood, limped to the wall, took down the old sinew-wrapped bow, held it and looked at it a while, set it before his son, and said: "Your grandpa's. You take it."

Xiaoman started. "…Dad, that sounds like swearing."

"Don't talk nonsense." His father pushed the bow into his arms. "Your grandpa's bow."

Xiaoman held the bow. Seventeen strips of sinew on its back; the one that had come loose in autumn, pressed back by him, his father had since rewound with new sinew, tight. He looked up. "Dad, and home —"

"Home's got me," his father said. "Knee's no good, hands still are; two mu of land won't let us starve."

His father said: "You've drawn this bow once. Drew it well." A pause. "From now on you draw it alone. Alone, there's nobody behind you saying read the wind first. You'll have to say it yourself."

Xiaoman said, "First read the wind, then the deer."

His father said, "Mm." He thought, and went on: "There's one more line I never told you."

Xiaoman pricked up his ears.

His father said, "If you can't read the wind, don't draw." He pressed the back of the bow with his hand. "How many arrows can one bow loose in a lifetime? What's loosed can't be called back. Not drawing is no shame."

His father paused, and went on: "At an immortal sect, keep their rules. Be honest. Don't fight with people —"

Xiaoman's mother said, "Husband."

His father said no more.

His mother took a little cloth bundle from her coat and pressed it into Xiaoman's hand. Xiaoman opened it: a sewing kit — a thimble, three needles, a reel of black thread, a reel of white, the needles stuck in a scrap of cloth, neat and tidy. And a purse, sewn of blue cloth, the stitches fine and close, a red cord through the mouth.

The purse was empty.

His mother said: "Needle and thread. When your clothes tear, mend them yourself." She tapped the purse with a finger. "The purse is empty. You fill it yourself."

His mother looked at him and said: "Of your father's words, listen to half."

His father coughed on the edge of the kang. His mother ignored him.

"Keep the rules — right. Be honest — honest with good people. Don't fight with people —" here she stopped. She reached out and turned his collar straight. That collar she'd unpicked and resewn a few days before, turned so the lining faced out, which made it look a bit newer. She turned the collar straight, and smoothed it, smoothed it flat, and only then said:

"If you can win, then fight."

The room went quiet. The lamp flame jumped.

Xiaoman looked at his mother. His mother looked back, her face showing nothing, as if saying the porridge was a bit thin today. But the hand that had turned his collar, once done, didn't draw back at once; it rested on his shoulder a moment.

Xiaoman later went many places, met many people, heard many grand principles from many great men. But the words that taught him how to live in this life came to just these: *If you can win, then fight.*

label.en: The sixth of the ninth month: set off for the Si River

exits.means: sets off for the trials at the temple

story.zh:
走的那天，是九月初六，天还没亮。

舅舅在济世堂告了三天假，头天夜里便到了，要一路送他走到泗水；他爹送他们到县城。他娘没有送，她说家里得有人看着灶。她站在老槐树底下，两只手拢在袖子里，一动不动，像去年秋天那样。

临走前，他娘塞给他一个布包，布包里是四张饼。

饼是前一夜烙的。小满半夜醒来，看见灶间的油灯亮着——那灯芯头一回没掐短，火苗有指头那么大——他娘站在灶前，一张一张地烙，烙好一张，拿布盖着，再烙下一张。那面是家里最后的一点白面，比去年秋天进山那一回剩的还少。他娘把面揉了又揉，擀得极薄，薄得对着灯看，能看见灯苗。

他娘道：「路上吃。一天一张，吃到泗水。」

小满数了数，四张。他道：「娘，到泗水要几天？」

他娘道：「三天。」

小满道：「那多了一张。」

他娘道：「打不过，就跑。跑饿了，吃那一张。」

小满把布包揣进怀里，贴着胸口那块木牌。他隔着衣裳按了按，心里说：你还欠我一张饼，别忘了。

他娘又塞给他一样东西，是一个小本子。那本子是拿舅舅开春带来的那包红糖的包纸订起来的，一张一张裁得方方正正，拿麻线在一边缝了，封皮上还透着一点红糖的甜味。他娘道：「一个人进山门，身上没个账本可不行。」小满翻开来看，里头一个字也没有。他娘道：「空的。你自己记。」

一个空钱袋，一个空本子。小满心想，他娘给他的东西，都是空的，都要他自己去装满。

小满背着弓，揣着针线、空钱袋、空本子和四张饼，走过老槐树的时候，停了一停。他回头看了一眼。

老槐树底下，只有他娘一个人。她的一只手从袖子里抬了起来，停在半空里，没有挥，也没有放下来。小满认得那只手——那一天碗碎的时候，他娘伸出去捞碗，也是这样停在半空里的。

他转过身，跟着他爹和舅舅，往村外走去。他爹走在最前头，一瘸一拐的。走出村口的那一刻，胸口那块木牌，轻轻地，暖了一下。

他小声道：「嗯。走了。」

身后，天边刚刚发白。石坳村的炊烟，一缕一缕，升了起来。
story.en:
The day he left was the sixth of the ninth month, before dawn.

His uncle had taken three days' leave from the Jishi Hall and arrived the night before, to walk him all the way to the Si River; his father would see them as far as the county town. His mother wasn't coming; someone had to mind the stove, she said. She stood under the old locust, both hands tucked in her sleeves, motionless, as she had the autumn before.

Before he left his mother pressed a cloth bundle on him; in it were four flatbreads.

They'd been made the night before. Xiaoman had woken in the middle of the night and seen the kitchen lamp lit — for the first time the wick not pinched short, the flame the size of a finger — and his mother at the stove making them one by one, each one covered with a cloth when done before she made the next. The flour was the last white flour in the house, less even than was left the autumn before when they went into the mountains. His mother had kneaded it and kneaded it and rolled it very thin, so thin you could see the flame through it held up to the lamp.

His mother said: "For the road. One a day, till you get to the Si River."

Xiaoman counted: four. "Mum, how many days to the Si River?"

His mother said, "Three."

Xiaoman said, "Then there's one too many."

His mother said, "If you can't win, run. When running makes you hungry, eat that one."

Xiaoman tucked the bundle inside his jacket, against the token at his chest. He pressed it through his clothes and said in his heart: you still owe me a flatbread; don't forget.

His mother pressed something else on him: a little notebook. It was made from the wrapping paper of the brown sugar his uncle had brought in spring, the sheets cut square and sewn along one edge with hemp thread, the cover still faintly sweet with sugar. His mother said, "Going through a temple gate alone, you can't be without an account book." Xiaoman opened it; not a word inside. His mother said, "It's empty. You write it."

An empty purse, an empty notebook. Xiaoman thought: everything his mother gave him was empty, all for him to fill himself.

Xiaoman, with the bow on his back and the sewing kit, the empty purse, the empty notebook and four flatbreads in his jacket, stopped as he passed the old locust. He looked back.

Under the old locust there was only his mother. One of her hands had come up out of her sleeve and stopped in mid-air — not waving, not lowered. Xiaoman knew that hand: the day the bowl broke, when his mother reached to catch it, her hand had stopped in mid-air just like this.

He turned and followed his father and his uncle out of the village. His father walked in front, limping. The moment they passed out of the village gate, the token at his chest warmed, gently.

He said softly: "Mm. We're off."

Behind him the sky was just going white at the edge. The cooking smoke of Shi'ao Village rose up, one thread after another.
